extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and critics interested in novel form and construction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on designing and judging the form of long fiction (the novel), emphasizing unity of subject, economy of material, point of view, scope, and the integration of episodes into an overall design. Uses Tolstoy's War and Peace as a primary example of strengths and failures of novel form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear single subject / unity
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject, one and whole and irreducible — a novel cannot begin to take shape till it has this for its support. If it cannot be put into a phrase it is no subject for a novel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subject should be expressible succinctly (the author suggests that the subject can be put into a phrase or 'ten words'). Form depends on the subject; without a definite subject there is nothing to be said of the form. Anti-pattern: diffuse or multiple unnamed subjects that prevent a coherent design (example: War and Peace's competing lines of life-cycle vs. national saga).

rubrics_metrics.name: Form must coincide with the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The best form is that which makes the most of its subject — the well-made book is the book in which the subject and the form coincide and are indistinguishable — the book in which the matter is all used up in the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a form that expresses all the matter; when form and subject disagree, there will be superfluous material or missing essentials. Evaluation: judge whether the form 'makes the most' of the subject or leaves material unused or misplaced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of material — avoid waste
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy's novel is wasteful of its subject; the importation of another and an irrelevant story damages the clarity and relief of the primary theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All material should serve the core subject. Anti-patterns: interpolated, irrelevant episodes or themes that divert resources from the principal story. Example: War and Peace importing an extensive national-saga material that weakens its life-cycle story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence of a clear centre / unifying principle
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel needs a centre; without it the general shape fails to satisfy the eye. Tolstoy's work is criticized for having 'no centre'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design a unifying centre (a controlling idea, subject, or structural principle) that ties disparate parts together. Check whether the author attempts to gather multiple designs into one or simply proceeds complacently without a unifying intention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent development from the heart of the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Is this proceeding of the author the right one, the best for the subject? Is it possible to conceive and to name a better?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At each turn ask whether a development or digression advances the subject or contradicts it. Look for flaws, breaks, or divergences that suggest the treatment has 'diverged from the line of its true development.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid coupling incompatible large themes (don't write two novels at once)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two such novels caught up together and written out in a couple of thousand pages, inadvertently mixed and entangled — an oversight that can happen even to geniuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to pursue two grand, incommensurate narratives in the same work unless you have a deliberate scheme to unify them. Anti-pattern: alternating whole-book-scale themes with no principle of unity (example: simultaneous epic of life-cycle and national saga).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid didactic interruptions / authorial pamphleteering
rubrics_metrics.description: He is capable of thrusting into his book interminable chapters of comment and explanation, chapters in the manner of a controversial pamphlet, lest the argument of his drama should be missed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid long expository or argumentative digressions that break narrative flow. Reader behavior: such passages often lead readers to skip pages. Prefer letting the story show the idea through action and character rather than explicit polemic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view / focalization should be chosen and used consistently
rubrics_metrics.description: The predominant point of view in some parts is the author's own independent storyteller; in others the story is presented through the minds of characters (Peter, Andrew, Nicholas), with Tolstoy effaced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the narrative will rely on authorial, omniscient narration or on character-centered focalization, and maintain a coherent method. Anti-pattern: random switching between an intrusive narrator and intimate character focalization, producing uneven effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate episodic material into the central story
rubrics_metrics.description: Battle-scenes and other large episodes should belong to the lives of central characters or else constitute the principal story; otherwise they screen or distract from the main life-story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When including episodic material (battles, historical set-pieces), either frame it through the experience of central characters so it enriches their arc, or ensure it is genuinely the central material. Avoid scenes narrated on the author's authority that have no bearing on the focal characters' development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate scope and population for the theme
rubrics_metrics.description: Such a subject (e.g., the march of life and generational change) could not be treated at all without a generous amount of room for its needs; it requires a big and various population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the novel's scale (number of characters, temporal and spatial scope) to the demands of the subject. Provide enough population and 'open world' feeling when the theme is representative/universal; conversely, restrict scope for an intense, interior fable. Anti-pattern: insufficient or excessive world for the chosen theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should exemplify the subject (representative truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are sought and chosen for the clarity with which the drama is embodied in them; their attachment to the general drama of life must be felt and understood — they should not seem merely exceptional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and shape characters so they elucidate the theme (typical truth), rather than standing out as unrelated curiosities. Ensure their relation to the wider world and to the theme is clear and convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your subject before deciding the form
rubrics_metrics.description: The form of the book depends on it, and until it is known there is nothing to be said of the form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine the novel's subject early; let that discovery drive decisions about structure, scope, and narrative method. Anti-pattern: experimenting with form before the subject is settled, producing aimless or incoherent structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete development — avoid fragmentary, unfinished themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither of the two competing stories is finished; neither is given its full development, for all the size of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the chosen subject receives full, satisfying development and climax. Large-scale novels especially must not treat their themes fragmentarily; lack of completion is a structural failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting and the sense of space deliberately (open world vs enclosed theatre)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy's people move in an atmosphere that knows no limit — an open sky and receding crowd — while Dostoevsky intensifies by shutting off the world with an enclosing darkness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the fable requires a vast open world (creating universality and breadth) or an enclosed, intensified setting (focusing inner life). Convey scope by characters' freedom and movement rather than mere descriptive padding when aiming for breadth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and composure should support, not mask, formal unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Tolstoy's assurance and luminous simplicity can mask incongruity of design; style may give an air of lucidity but cannot substitute for a true centre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prose style to enhance clarity and cohesion, but beware that elegant style can conceal structural defects; criticism should look beneath a pleasing surface to the underlying unity and economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader reconstruction as a test of form
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader recreates the book; if the recreated book melts away or falls to pieces when re-examined, the form has failed. The hours of the author's labour are lived again by the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use re-readings and critical reconstruction — attempting to 'recreate' the design from parts — to test whether form holds together. A robust form will survive scrutiny; a weak one will reveal gaps, incongruities, or wasted matter.
